patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Germany → South Africa: Fr Georg Kerkhoff (extradited back); Germany → South America: Jesuit Fr Wolfgang S.; Essen → Munich: Fr Peter Hullermann.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The map draws 34 documented moves recorded by inquiries, courts and the institutions' own files, and colors every country that sent or received an abuser. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Odenwaldschule: first report 1998, first action 2010 (12 years). Victims came forward 1998 and Frankfurter Rundschau reported Nov 1999; promised review never took place; prosecutors dropped the case as time-barred Lügde campsite: first report 2016, first action 2019 (3 years). Police received two tips in 2016; youth office placed a foster child with the main offender; 155 evidence items vanished from a police office Peter Hullermann (Munich): first report 1979, first action 1986 (7 years). Accepted into Munich in 1980 under Cardinal Ratzinger for therapy and given pastoral work, abused again
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases the sources date both the first complaint that reached police, a church, an employer or officials, and the first conviction, charge or official finding. The middle wait is 12.0 years. A pupil told police about the MP Cyril Smith in 1968 and was told Smith was "a very important, powerful man"; in 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged and had been assured in 1970 that he would not be. Complaints about Jimmy Savile reached police from 1958; investigations in his lifetime brought no charges. Athletes complained about Larry Nassar from 1997. Each country is colored by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Deadlines, lobbying and bankruptcy
patterns.role_note: 2013: Bundestag (March 2013) extended civil limitation for sexual abuse claims from 3 to 30 years (s.197 BGB); criminal limitation starts running only at victim's 21st birthday (s.78b StGB). Not retroactive for already time-barred claims
patterns.pattern_summary: Most survivors disclose decades later, after the legal deadline to sue or prosecute has passed. Where legislatures tried to lift those deadlines, the institutions facing claims lobbied against it, and when the deadlines fell, many filed for bankruptcy. The Catholic Church spent about $10.6 million lobbying in eight northeastern US states from 2011 to 2018; in Pennsylvania, which still has no window for old claims, the Catholic Conference spent over $7.6 million and the insurance federation nearly $20.7 million from 2014 to 2024. From 2004 to 2025, 40 US Catholic dioceses and orders filed for bankruptcy, several within hours or days of a trial, a deposition or a new law.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2010: Round Table on Sexual Child Abuse (Runder Tisch), federal government, 24 Mar 2010 - final report 30 Nov 2011; Independent Commissioner (UBSKM) from 2010. Set up after the January 2010 Canisius-Kolleg revelations; chaired by three federal ministers
patterns.pattern_summary: Official inquiries into institutional child abuse came in waves: Canada and Ireland first (Hughes, 1989; the Ryan commission, 1999–2009), the United States in 2002–2004, most of western Europe after 2010, Australia's Royal Commission 2013–2017, then France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland from 2021. Where inquiries used population surveys, the numbers were far above church records: about 216,000 minors abused by French clergy and religious since 1950, against about 3,000 identified before. Many "national" studies were commissioned by the church itself. Italy, Brazil, the Philippines and India, with some of the largest Catholic populations, have no national inquiry in the sources reached.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Paul Schäfer / Colonia Dignidad (2019): Hopp living in Germany; investigation dropped
patterns.pattern_summary: When the accused belongs to another state, a diplomatic service or an army, prosecution depends on that state. UN peacekeepers fall under their own country's courts: at least 134 Sri Lankan soldiers were accused of abusing nine Haitian children in 2004–2007 and none was convicted. The Holy See recalled its nuncio to the Dominican Republic, Józef Wesołowski, and told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow his extradition. South Korea's court refused to send the Welcome to Video operator to the United States. Morocco's king pardoned a Spanish child rapist as a gesture to Spain. Israel's deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments that kept Malka Leifer from extradition for years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 2 documented adoption flows into Germany on this map.
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Romania (1990s), Guatemala (until 2007–08), Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia (banned 2018) and others followed, each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children were carried out by states, as policy. Argentina's junta took about 500 babies from detained mothers in 1976–83 (a 2012 court found a "systematic plan"; 140 grandchildren had been identified by July 2025). Under Franco, children were taken from Republican and later unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children into residential schools and non-Indigenous families; Denmark sent Greenlandic children to Danish families in 1951; France moved children from Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported Ukrainian children; the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over it.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 1993: Germany: extraterritorial jurisdiction for sexual abuse of children abroad (s.5 no.8 StGB), even where the act is legal at the place of the offence
patterns.pattern_summary: Child sex tourism followed enforcement around the map. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. When Manila closed Ermita in 1992, businesses moved to Angeles City. Offenders' home countries passed laws to prosecute their citizens for abuse abroad (Germany 1993, Australia 1994, Canada 1997, Japan 1999, the US PROTECT Act 2003). Then the trade moved online: in the Philippines, street and establishment child sex trafficking fell 79–86% in targeted cities (2006–2016), while monthly Philippine internet addresses used for child sexual exploitation rose more than twelvefold (2014–2017).

patterns.pattern: When spies, soldiers and police are named
patterns.role: Proven link to a state service
patterns.role_note: Germany acknowledges failures over Colonia Dignidad (proven link to a state service). 'Kentler experiment' — Berlin youth office placed children with paedophile foster fathers (proven link to a state service).
patterns.pattern_summary: Claims that intelligence services run or protect child-abuse networks are common. The records sort them into what was proven, what was disproved and what is still only claimed. Proven: the founder of Colonia Dignidad in Chile was convicted of abusing children there and charged with aiding the Pinochet regime, which Chilean officials say used the colony to torture opponents, and Germany admitted its embassy looked away. West Berlin's youth authorities placed boys with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, from the late 1960s, on a psychologist's advice. US troops in Afghanistan were told not to intervene when allied commanders abused boys. UN police monitors and US contractors in Bosnia bought trafficked girls. The FBI and Australian police ran abuse sites for weeks to months to identify users. Disproved: the Kincora inquiry found no evidence MI5 used the home for blackmail; the Met's Operation Midland "VIP ring" was invented by a man later jailed for it. Claimed, not established: that Jeffrey Epstein worked for an intelligence agency.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 18,401 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (6% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse runs on ordinary infrastructure: hosting companies, payment systems and the largest social platforms. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation found most of the abuse material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports to the US CyberTipline rose from 4,560 in 1998 to over 36 million in 2023, then fell after Meta encrypted its messages, not because abuse fell. Payments for livestreamed abuse run from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines; Australia's Westpac agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty in 2020 that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. Backpage earned more than $500 million from ads used to sell children before it was shut in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: 'Kentler experiment' — Berlin youth office placed children with paedophile foster fathers; Lügde campsite abuse — youth office placed foster child with offender; Sebastian Edathy (Bundestag) — images of naked minors; case closed on payment; Germany acknowledges failures over Colonia Dignidad.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 242 cases on this map, police, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part, or a court or inquiry found they ignored, buried or obstructed it. In Rotherham the Jay report found about 1,400 children exploited from 1997 to 2013 and called the council's and police's failures "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. A senior Australian police officer in 1972 offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. North Wales police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, Puebla police arrested the journalist who exposed a Cancún abuse ring, and leaked calls recorded the state governor discussing her jailing; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Romania–UK 'loverboy' network dismantled — 21 arrested (Eurojust, 2020)
cases.who: Romanian organized criminal group using the 'loverboy' method
cases.what: On 9 September 2020 a Romanian–UK Joint Investigation Team supported by Eurojust arrested 21 members of a hierarchical group active since 2009 that seduced vulnerable Romanian girls with false promises of relationships, exploited minors in prostitution in Romania until they turned 18, and then moved them to the UK, Ireland and Germany. Thirty-two house searches were carried out (23 in Romania, 9 in the UK). Eurojust said Romania and the UK had cooperated in 76 trafficking investigations in four years.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Colonia Dignidad (Chile) — child sexual abuse by Paul Schäfer; DINA detention and torture site
cases.who: Colonia Dignidad sect led by Paul Schäfer; Chile's secret police DINA; West German embassy
cases.what: Paul Schäfer, a former Nazi army corporal wanted in Germany on child abuse charges, founded the Colonia Dignidad commune in southern Chile in 1961. Chilean officials believe the colony was used as a centre for torture of opponents of the Pinochet dictatorship between 1973 and 1990, and Schäfer was charged with aiding the regime. The colony recruited children from local farms into its free school and clinic; an investigation opened only after Chilean mothers complained in 1997. Schäfer fled to Argentina, was arrested there in March 2005 and returned to Chile, and on 24–25 May 2006 a Chilean court sentenced him to 20 years for sexually abusing 25 children; with further convictions for torture, weapons and a murder his sentences totalled 33 years. He died in prison in 2010. The colony's doctor, Hartmut Hopp, was convicted in Chile in 2011 of 16 counts of aiding child sexual abuse.
cases.cover_up: In 1966 a teenager who fled took refuge at the West German embassy; the embassy sent a delegation and said it found no evidence. German diplomats praised it as a 'model colony'. Federal President Gauck said in July 2016 that German diplomats had for years looked away; Foreign Minister Steinmeier in April 2016 shortened the closure period of Foreign Office files from 30 to 20 years to release them. Schäfer fled in 1997 and was caught in Argentina in March 2005.

cases.title: Odenwaldschule, Heppenheim — abuse by headmaster Gerold Becker and teachers
cases.who: Odenwaldschule (private, state-recognised progressive boarding school); headmaster Gerold Becker, music teacher Wolfgang Held
cases.what: Lawyers Claudia Burgsmüller and Brigitte Tilmann, a former judge, were called in by the school to investigate; their 2010 report identified more than a dozen perpetrators, with former headmaster Gerold Becker and a music teacher named as the main abusers from the late 1960s, and 17 witnesses testifying against Becker. Later counts put the victims at at least 132 pupils abused by teachers between the 1960s and 1990s; the victims' association says at least 20 teachers were responsible. The abuse, long covered up, became widely public in 2010; pupil numbers and funding fell and in April 2015 the school's sponsoring association announced its closure. Becker also appears in the Hildesheim research as a figure in the Kentler network.
cases.cover_up: After victims came forward in 1998 and the Frankfurter Rundschau reported it in November 1999, a promised review did not take place; prosecutors in Darmstadt dropped the case under the statute of limitations. Becker died in 2010 without facing legal consequences.

cases.title: MHG study — German Bishops' Conference
cases.who: German Catholic dioceses
cases.what: The study by researchers from Mannheim, Heidelberg and Giessen, commissioned by the German Bishops' Conference and presented on 25 September 2018, found 1,670 clerics (4.4% of clergy) accused of abusing 3,677 minors between 1946 and 2014. The authors called the figures conservative and found that personnel files had been destroyed or manipulated.
cases.cover_up: Researchers found personnel files had been destroyed or manipulated

cases.title: Germany acknowledges failures over Colonia Dignidad
cases.who: German Foreign Office; Colonia Dignidad
cases.what: In April 2016 Germany released Foreign Office files from 1986–1996 and the foreign minister admitted diplomats had failed colony residents, including abused children. In 2017 the Bundestag formally acknowledged German responsibility and asked the government to plan an investigation, memorial and help for victims; in 2019 Germany announced compensation payments to victims.
cases.cover_up: Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier said in April 2016 that 'over the course of many years, from the 60s to the 80s, German diplomats at best looked away' and that the embassy failed to shield Germans at the colony.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

cases.title: 'Kentler experiment' — Berlin youth office placed children with paedophile foster fathers
cases.who: Berlin Senate youth administration and state youth office (Landesjugendamt); sexologist Helmut Kentler (Pädagogisches Zentrum Berlin, later TU Hannover); network incl. Gerold Becker of the Odenwaldschule
cases.what: From the late 1960s (Kentler held a post at the Senate's Pädagogisches Zentrum from 1967 to 1976) West Berlin youth authorities, on the advice of Helmut Kentler, placed homeless boys and other children with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, as a form of 'resocialisation'. University of Hildesheim reports (2020 and final report 22 February 2024) reconstructed a nationwide network in science, youth welfare and administration that supported, legitimised or tolerated paedophile positions and sexual violence, continuing beyond 2000. Some children were about five years old when placed. Berlin says known victims have received compensation.
cases.cover_up: University of Hildesheim researchers found the abuse was carried out and institutionalised under the responsibility of the Landesjugendamt and the Berlin Senate administration; Kentler died in 2008 without prosecution.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Elysium darknet platform
cases.who: Elysium (darknet forum and chats, over 87,000 members)
cases.what: Elysium existed from late 2016 and was used to exchange abuse material and to arrange the sexual abuse of children; it had German, French, Spanish and Italian chat groups. German prosecutors (ZIT Frankfurt) and the BKA shut it down in June 2017 after Australian police passed on a lead; 14 suspects were arrested, 12 suspected of abusing children themselves. On 7 March 2019 the Limburg court sentenced four men to between 3 years 10 months and 9 years 9 months, with preventive detention for the main administrator.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Germany; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.what: Berlin youth authorities placed children with men known to be paedophiles as foster fathers, including outside Berlin; the Hildesheim report names Hannover and other Lower Saxony locations as network nodes.

flows.what: Schäfer fled abuse accusations in Germany in 1961 and the colony kept 'importing' children.

cases.title: Fr Johannes Rivoire — Oblate in Nunavut, never extradited from France
cases.who: Oblates of Mary Immaculate (OMI Lacombe Canada; Oblates of France)
cases.what: French Oblate Johannes Rivoire worked in the Canadian North from 1959 to 1993. He faced at least three sexual-abuse charges (1998 warrant) concerning Inuit children in Arviat, Rankin Inlet and Naujaat, and a 2022 warrant for indecent assault on a girl in Arviat and Whale Cove between 1974 and 1979. A March 2024 review by retired Quebec justice André Denis, commissioned by the Oblates, concluded on the preponderance of evidence that he assaulted six children. Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami called his death without trial in April 2024 'a systemic failure of nation states and religious institutions'.
cases.cover_up: He left for France in January 1993; a Canadian arrest warrant followed in 1998 and charges were later stayed. A 2022 warrant led to an extradition request that French authorities denied. The 2024 Denis review found the RCMP never contacted the Oblates when charges were laid. In February 2024 the Vatican ruled against his dismissal. He died in France in 2024 without trial.

cases.title: Joël Le Scouarnec — surgeon convicted for 299 victims
cases.who: Joël Le Scouarnec (surgeon); hospitals and medical regulators
cases.what: Le Scouarnec, a surgeon in western France, was convicted in Saintes in December 2020 of raping and sexually assaulting four children, including two of his nieces (15 years). At his second trial in Vannes he admitted abusing all 299 victims, mostly hospital patients, many under anaesthesia or waking from surgery, between 1989 and 2014; more than 250 were under 15. On 28 May 2025 the court sentenced him to the maximum 20 years. He is not part of an elite network; included as a professional whose standing protected him (setting is debatable — could be moved to 'care').
cases.cover_up: The FBI traced his downloading of abuse images in 2004; his 2005 conviction (4 months suspended) brought no restriction on practice. Prosecutors did not alert medical authorities; the regional medical body found no breach in 2006; a 2007 warning to the health ministry brought no action; a hospital hired him in 2008 knowing of the conviction.

cases.title: CIASE (Sauvé Commission) — Catholic Church in France
cases.who: Catholic Church in France (commissioned by bishops and religious orders)
cases.what: The Independent Commission on Sexual Abuse in the Church, chaired by Jean-Marc Sauvé, reported on 5 October 2021. Using a population survey, it estimated about 216,000 people were abused as minors by clergy and religious from 1950 to 2020, and about 330,000 including lay people working in church institutions. Archive research put the number of abusive clergy and religious at 2,900 to 3,200, a floor of 2.5% to 2.8% of the roughly 115,000 who served, and it described the abuse as massive and its causes as systemic.
cases.cover_up: Commission called the abuse 'massive' and 'systemic' and said the church must accept institutional responsibility

cases.title: French Operation Sangaris soldiers — alleged abuse of children, Bangui
cases.who: French army, Operation Sangaris (not under UN command)
cases.what: An internal UN document revealed by The Guardian in April 2015 recorded interviews with six boys aged 9 to 13 who said French soldiers of Operation Sangaris had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014 at the displaced persons' camp at Bangui's M'Poko airport, in exchange for food rations. The Paris prosecutor had opened a preliminary inquiry in July 2014; the investigation eventually covered accusations by fifteen children, most interviewed in Bangui in 2015 and 2016. In January 2018 French investigating judges dismissed the case (non-lieu) for lack of sufficient charges, citing inconsistencies in testimony; the prosecutor said 'it cannot be affirmed at the end of the investigation that no sexual abuse was committed'. No soldier was charged.
cases.cover_up: The internal UN report was not passed to French authorities by the UN; the UN official who passed it on (Anders Kompass) was suspended and resigned in 2016 in protest at impunity.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: France — Children of Creuse: 2,015 Réunionese children moved to mainland France
cases.who: French state social services (DDASS); scheme led by Réunion MP Michel Debré
cases.what: Between 1963 and 1982 the French state took roughly 2,000 children from Réunion who had been made wards of the state and sent them to depopulating rural departments of mainland France such as Creuse, promising their families a good education and a better future. Some were adopted; others stayed in homes or were made to work on farms. On 18 February 2014 the National Assembly passed a resolution stating that the state had failed in its moral responsibility towards these wards and that their right to maintain ties with their families had been insufficiently protected. No compensation payments have been planned.

cases.title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

cases.title: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
cases.who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
cases.what: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

cases.title: Vietnam — Operation Babylift (1975): not all children were orphans
cases.who: US government (Military Airlift Command); Holt International, Friends of Children of Viet Nam, Friends For All Children and other agencies
cases.what: In April 1975, as South Vietnam was falling, President Ford directed that a $2 million special foreign aid fund be used to fly 2,000 South Vietnamese orphans to the United States; Wikipedia, citing several sources, gives a total of over 3,300 children airlifted. The first flight, a C-5 cargo plane, crash-landed shortly after take-off on 4 April 1975, killing many of the children on board (78, according to US Defense Intelligence Agency figures cited by Wikipedia). A lawsuit filed against Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, the federal government and the adoption agencies argued that many of the children were not orphans and had been given up under duress during wartime; poor families sometimes placed children in orphanages without intending to give them up, and many adoption records lacked parental consent.

cases.title: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
cases.who: Salvadoran armed forces
cases.what: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cases.cover_up: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.

cases.title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

cases.title: Chad — Zoé's Ark tries to fly 103 children to France (convicted 2007)
cases.who: French charity L'Arche de Zoé (founder Éric Breteau)
cases.what: In October 2007 members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were detained in Chad as they tried to fly 103 children to France; the charity said they were orphans from Sudan's Darfur region, but authorities found most were from Chad and not orphans. On 26 December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children and sentenced them to eight years' forced labour, and ordered each to pay €60,000 to each of the 103 children; a Chadian and a Sudanese defendant got four years and two Chadians were acquitted. The six were transferred to France, and Chad's President Idriss Déby pardoned them at the end of March 2008.

cases.title: France — state report finds 'illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption
cases.who: French government and adoption associations
cases.what: In March 2024 France released an assessment acknowledging that its government had long known of 'the existence of illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption, and that diplomatic and association archives showed these practices existed in countries over long periods. France received 11,165 Korean children 1968–2008 among others.
cases.cover_up: The report said public authorities were alerted early, including at the highest levels, and were late in taking action.

cases.title: Freedom Hosting — Tor host for Lolita City and other abuse sites
cases.who: Freedom Hosting (Eric Eoin Marques, convicted)
cases.what: Freedom Hosting was a free anonymous dark web hosting service that ran from July 2008 to July 2013 and hosted over 200 child exploitation websites, including Lolita City, which Anonymous had attacked in 2011. The operator, Eric Eoin Marques, was arrested in Dublin in early August 2013 on a US warrant; the FBI accused him of being 'the largest facilitator of child porn on the planet'. After Ireland's Supreme Court dismissed his challenge in March 2019 he was extradited, pleaded guilty on 6 February 2020 to conspiracy to advertise child sexual abuse material, and on 16 September 2021 was sentenced to 27 years. DOJ said the sites held millions of images and videos, over 1.97 million not previously known to law enforcement.
cases.cover_up: Extradition from Ireland took from 2013 to 2019 through appeals.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role_note: 18,612 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman).
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)

In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

cases.title: Ukraine — Ukrainian children given Russian citizenship and adopted into Russian families
cases.who: Russian state; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
cases.what: On 30 May 2022 President Putin signed a decree easing Russian citizenship for Ukrainian children so they could be adopted by Russian families; Russia created a register of families wishing to adopt Ukrainian children and paid families per adopted child granted citizenship. Lvova-Belova said she had adopted a child from Mariupol herself. On 17 March 2023 the ICC issued arrest warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova for unlawful deportation and transfer of children. Yale HRL (14 February 2023) documented a 'systematic' programme of re-education and adoption. (Deportations and camps are recorded by the conflict agent; this record covers the adoption element.)

cases.title: Russia — deportation and transfer of Ukrainian children; ICC warrants for Putin and Lvova-Belova
cases.who: Russian state: President Vladimir Putin; Children's Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova
cases.what: On 17 March 2023 ICC Pre-Trial Chamber II issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova for the war crimes of unlawful deportation and unlawful transfer of children from occupied Ukraine to Russia, committed from at least 24 February 2022. The UN Commission of Inquiry found a transfer of 31 children in May 2022 was unlawful deportation and a war crime; Lvova-Belova's own bulletin said 380 orphans had been placed with Russian foster families and about 2,000 children from institutions transferred in February 2022. Yale's Humanitarian Research Lab reported in February 2023 at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea holding at least 6,000 Ukrainian children for 're-education'.

cases.title: Ukraine — UN-verified abduction of children by Russian armed forces and authorities (2022–2023)
cases.who: Russian armed forces, affiliated armed groups and Russian authorities in occupied territories
cases.what: The UN Secretary-General verified the abduction, beginning in 2022 and continuing into 2023, of 122 children (75 boys, 47 girls) attributed to Russian armed forces, affiliated armed groups and Russian authorities in occupied Ukrainian territories; 91 abductions by Russian armed forces had been verified for 2022. The 2025 report welcomed the reunification of two of these children and said the whereabouts of the rest remained unknown.

cases.title: Ukraine orphanages as a 'recruitment tool' for traffickers — Disability Rights International 'No Way Home'
cases.who: Ukrainian state orphanages, boarding schools and institutions for children with disabilities
cases.what: Disability Rights International investigated 33 institutions between 2012 and 2015 and published 'No Way Home' in 2015. La Strada Ukraine told DRI that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution is 'the most typical scheme' and that sexual exploitation in institutions typically begins around age 13, often instigated by staff; an IOM counter-trafficking coordinator called orphanages a direct feeder to domestic and international trafficking and said most documented cases originate in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. DRI concluded that the orphanage system serves as a recruitment tool for traffickers.

cases.title: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
cases.who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and clients; 18 IPTF monitors who purchased women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges went home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. On 2 August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found DynCorp had unfairly dismissed IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking.
cases.cover_up: Immunity: IPTF monitors were repatriated rather than prosecuted (18 returned home; HRW found no prosecution by Nov 2002); DynCorp contractors were sent home, preventing their use as witnesses; DynCorp fired whistleblower Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001.

cases.title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
cases.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cases.what: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.
cases.cover_up: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

cases.title: Ukraine — rape and sexual violence by Russian forces incl. children (UN Commission of Inquiry)
cases.who: Russian armed forces and authorities
cases.what: The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine found that Russian authorities committed the war crimes of rape and other sexual violence; cases it investigated included a 16-year-old girl, and in September 2022 it said it had documented children raped, tortured and unlawfully confined. Ukraine's official Children of War platform records 23 children sexually abused, according to the Office of the Prosecutor General.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Ukraine — wartime risk to evacuated institutional children; officials allegedly complicit (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Criminal networks; some institution officials
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says child sex trafficking in Ukraine is underreported and criminals are trying to build online networks to exploit Ukrainian children internationally; children evacuated from at least 195 facilities, including those with disabilities, are at high risk; and Ukrainian refugee women and children are vulnerable in Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Bulgaria and the UK. Ukraine convicted 24 traffickers in 2024, only six with prison terms.
cases.cover_up: Officials of several state-run residential institutions were allegedly complicit or negligent in trafficking of children in their care; no complicit officials convicted for the eighth year running.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: New Zealand → Australia: Brother Bernard McGrath; New Zealand → Papua New Guinea: priests sent after allegations; Australia / New Zealand → Fiji: transferred clergy.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. Offenders' home countries passed laws to prosecute their citizens for abuse abroad (Germany 1993, Australia 1994, Canada 1997, Japan 1999, the US PROTECT Act 2003). cases.title: Royal Commission into Abuse in Care — Catholic institutions
cases.who: Catholic Church in Aotearoa New Zealand; St John of God Brothers at Marylands School
cases.what: The Royal Commission's final report, Whanaketia, published 24 July 2024, found about 200,000 people were abused in state and faith-based care from 1950 to 2019. It found Catholic responses inadequate, noting a 2020 church briefing that 14% of clergy were accused over 1950–1999, and singled out Marylands School in Christchurch for some of the highest levels of sexual abuse. It found abusers were transferred to other ministries and recommended an inquiry into priests sent to Papua New Guinea.
cases.cover_up: Church relied on psychiatrists' opinions to transfer abusers to other ministries where they reoffended; commission recommended investigating priests transferred to Papua New Guinea

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: Lake Alice Hospital Child and Adolescent Unit — torture finding
cases.who: Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital, child and adolescent unit; psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks
cases.what: Between 1972 and 1978, 362 children went through the child and adolescent unit at Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital; about half were Māori boys. Survivors described electric shocks without anaesthetic and painful paraldehyde injections used as punishment, and evidence was given of children being raped and sexually abused by staff and adult patients. In 2019 the UN Committee Against Torture found New Zealand had breached the Convention by failing to investigate properly; police opened a new investigation in 2020. Psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks denied abuse and was never criminally charged in New Zealand. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care found many of the children were tortured, and on 18 Dec 2024 the government announced NZ$150,000 redress per survivor and a new Crown apology explicitly acknowledging torture.
cases.cover_up: The Crown's internal policy refused to recognise the long-term effects of abuse, forcing complaints to the UN Committee Against Torture in 2019.

cases.title: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care — 'Whanaketia' final report
cases.who: State social welfare, disability, mental health, education, law-enforcement and faith-based care settings
cases.what: The final report, made public on 24 July 2024, found abuse was rife in state and faith-based care and that sexual abuse was commonplace, with abusers grooming people in care. It estimated 200,000 of about 655,000 people in care between 1950 and 2019 were abused; Māori were more likely to be abused. Commissioners Coral Shaw, Andrew Erueti and Paul Gibson made 138 recommendations, including a specialist investigation unit and an independent Care Safe Agency, and called it 'a national disgrace'.
cases.cover_up: Commissioners found the state failed to respond to signs of systemic abuse and neglect, and that by 2024 there had been very little progress on the redress system they recommended in 2021.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

flows.what: After allegations surfaced in 1977, the St John of God order transferred McGrath to Australia, where he later faced 252 charges; he was also convicted in New Zealand.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 1987: ban: Sri Lanka imposes temporary ban on foreign adoptions after baby-farm raid (20 newborns, 22 women found) 2017: scandal: Zembla documentary; Sri Lanka's health minister admits 1980s 'baby farms' and announces inquiry (September) 2020: acknowledgment: Swiss Federal Council acknowledges authorities' irregularities in Sri Lankan adoptions (also 2023) 2021: suspension: Netherlands suspension covers adoptions from all countries incl. Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil, Colombia
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Home country of accused troops or staff
patterns.role_note: Sri Lanka → Haiti: MINUSTAH contingent (offenders).
patterns.pattern_summary: Children in war zones and camps were abused by the people sent to protect or feed them. A 2002 UNHCR and Save the Children report documented aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food for sex with children. In Haiti, more than 100 Sri Lankan peacekeepers were sent home in 2007 over the abuse of children; none was convicted at home. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014–2016. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators in the WHO-led Ebola response in Congo (2018–2020), 21 of them WHO staff, with victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly allegation counts since 2004.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption; Seth Sevana children's home, Vavuniya — monk arrested, bail with NCPA consent; Anuradhapura children's home — probation officials arrested.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 242 cases on this map, police, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part, or a court or inquiry found they ignored, buried or obstructed it. patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting

patterns.pattern_summary: The map's documented record is thickest where people looked. cases.title: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti
cases.who: Sri Lanka Army contingent of the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH)
cases.what: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services concluded that 'acts of sexual exploitation and abuse (against children) were frequent and occurred usually at night, and at virtually every location where the contingent personnel were deployed', and said charges should include statutory rape. An Associated Press investigation in April 2017 found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring between 2004 and 2007; none was jailed.
cases.cover_up: Repatriation instead of prosecution: 114 Sri Lankan peacekeepers were sent home; Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts 'consensual' and nobody was jailed.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
cases.who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
cases.what: Swiss authorities soon realised that the placement of children for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, was also driven by economic interests and linked to organised child trafficking; decisions were often made on incomplete or falsified documents, and checks on foster families and on legal requirements were insufficient. From the 2010s, under pressure from groups such as Back to the Roots, intercountry adoptions from Tibet, Sri Lanka and India drew public attention. In 2018 the Federal Assembly commissioned a study on intercountry adoption; the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

cases.title: Seth Sevana children's home, Vavuniya — monk arrested, bail with NCPA consent
cases.who: Seth Sevana Lama Nivasa children's home (run by a Buddhist monk) housing war-affected Tamil children; National Child Protection Authority (NCPA)
cases.what: In October 2013 the head of a children's home in Vavuniya, a Buddhist monk, was arrested for sexually abusing a 9-year-old child, confirmed by medical evidence on 12 October 2013. The NCPA took custody of the other 22 children on 15 October 2013. Most children were war-affected Tamil children placed by poor families. Groundviews reported that complaints had reached the NCPA since 2010 and that the agency later supported his release on bail.
cases.cover_up: Complaints had been made to the NCPA since 2010; the arrest came only after protests by Vavuniya child protection officers. On 31 December 2013 the monk got unconditional bail after the Attorney General's Department, on NCPA instructions, told the court it had no objection; the NCPA did not submit the 22 children's reports to the court.

cases.title: Anuradhapura children's home — probation officials arrested
cases.who: North Central Provincial Department of Probation and Child Care Services
cases.what: After a media report on 8 January 2021 of illegal activity at a children's home near Anuradhapura and a complaint by the National Child Protection Authority on 16 January 2021, police arrested a former provincial Commissioner and a Senior Probation Officer of the Department of Probation and Child Care Services. They were accused over the treatment of a 17-year-old girl held at a counselling centre on court orders who was made to work as a cook in a children's home. They were granted bail by the Anuradhapura Magistrate's Court and the Attorney General's advice was sought on further action.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Melbourne → Israel (Malka Leifer flown out by her school).
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, brother, teacher or headmistress was found abusing children, the institution often moved them rather than calling the police: to another parish, another school, another state, or another continent. The Pennsylvania grand jury found bishops moved abusers between parishes; Bishop Mulkearns knew of Gerald Ridsdale's offending by late 1975 and kept reappointing him to new parishes; the Adass Israel School paid for Malka Leifer's 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel before police were told; the Makin review called John Smyth "a problem solved and exported to Africa".

cases.title: Malka Leifer — Adass Israel School, Melbourne
cases.who: Adass Israel School (ultra-Orthodox community school)
cases.what: Headmistress Malka Leifer abused pupils at Melbourne's ultra-Orthodox Adass Israel School between about 2003 and 2007. The school flew her to Israel in March 2008. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences involving at least eight pupils; she was arrested in Israel in August 2014, found in 2019 to have faked mental illness, and extradited on 25 January 2021. On 3 April 2023 a Melbourne jury found her guilty of 18 charges including rape, and in August 2023 she was sentenced to 15 years. In 2015 the Supreme Court of Victoria had ordered the school and Leifer to pay a former pupil about AU$1.27 million.
cases.cover_up: In March 2008, after a teacher confronted her, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children without telling police. In Israel, then deputy health minister Yaakov Litzman pressured ministry staff to alter psychiatric evaluations so she would appear unfit for extradition; her lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals.

cases.title: Yaakov Litzman — breach of trust for shielding Malka Leifer
cases.who: Israeli Ministry of Health; ultra-Orthodox Agudat Yisrael party
cases.what: Former Israeli health minister Yaakov Litzman signed a plea deal in January 2022 admitting breach of trust for pressuring Health Ministry employees to change psychiatric evaluations so that Malka Leifer would appear unfit to stand extradition trial. He resigned from the Knesset in June 2022 and on 8 August 2022 the Jerusalem Magistrate's Court sentenced him to eight months' probation and a fine of about US$900. Australian Jewish groups condemned the deal as lenient.
cases.cover_up: A government minister pressured ministry psychiatrists to alter evaluations of an extradition suspect.

cases.title: Israel — Yemenite, Mizrahi and Balkan children affair
cases.who: Israeli state health and immigration institutions
cases.what: More than 1,000 families, mostly immigrants from Yemen but also dozens from the Balkans, North Africa and other Middle Eastern countries, say babies taken to hospitals in Israel's early years disappeared after parents were told they had died; many believe they were given away for adoption. Three government inquiries since the 1960s concluded that most of the children died of disease and were buried without their parents being informed. In 2016 the government decided to put most of the inquiries' archives online. On 22 February 2021 the government expressed regret and approved a NIS 162 million compensation plan: NIS 150,000 for each child whose death was reported to the family at the time and NIS 200,000 for each child whose fate is unknown.

cases.title: Romania — post-1989 adoption trade and 2004 ban
cases.who: Private adoption agencies and intermediaries; Romanian authorities
cases.what: After Ceaușescu's fall, television images of about 100,000 children in orphanages led to an adoption boom; private agencies charged €7,500–25,000 and the system 'quickly became awash in corruption' (DW). Romania halted adoptions in June 1991 and, under EU pressure, passed a law in June 2004 banning all foreign adoptions except by grandparents. The European Parliament's rapporteur Baroness Emma Nicholson had criticised 'international adoption and child trafficking' in Romania. Romania's own HCCH return shows 458 intercountry adoptions in 2002, 332 in 2003, 2 in 2005 and 0 in 2006.

cases.title: Israel/Gaza — UN COI findings on sexual violence incl. against Palestinian boys and on 7 October
cases.who: Israeli security forces (detention and arrest); Hamas and other armed groups (7 October)
cases.what: The UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel found in June 2024 that Israeli security forces subjected Palestinians to sexual and gender-based violence including forced public nudity and sexualised torture, and that 'men and boys were targeted in particular ways'; it found gender persecution of Palestinian men and boys as a crime against humanity. It also found sexual violence was committed on 7 October 2023 at the Nova festival, Nahal Oz and several kibbutzim, and that 252 people, including 36 children, were taken hostage. Recorded only to the extent of these UN findings.

cases.title: China — Hunan orphanages bought trafficked babies for adoption (2005 convictions)
cases.who: Six state orphanages in Hunan; traffickers from Guangdong; local officials
cases.what: Six Hunan orphanages were found buying infants from traffickers who brought them from Guangdong, placing nearly 1,000 children with domestic and foreign families between 2002 and 2005. In 2005, according to Xinhua, 23 civil officials were fired; three traffickers were sentenced to 15 years and six others to 3–13 years.

cases.title: China — intercountry adoption programme ended (2024) after trafficking cases
cases.who: China Center for Children's Welfare and Adoption; state orphanages
cases.what: China opened intercountry adoption in 1992; about 160,000 children were sent abroad, peaking at almost 8,000 to the US in 2005. The programme came to depend increasingly on abuse, abduction and trafficking (New Yorker), including Hunan orphanages buying trafficked babies (2005). On 5 September 2024 the foreign ministry announced the end of the programme, except adoption by blood relatives or of a stepchild.

cases.title: China — Uyghur children separated from detained parents and placed in state boarding schools
cases.who: Chinese state authorities in Xinjiang
cases.what: As hundreds of thousands of Uyghur and other Muslim adults were detained in Xinjiang, the BBC reported in July 2019, with research by Adrian Zenz, a rapid campaign to build boarding schools and kindergartens with dormitory space, including $1.2bn spent in southern Xinjiang; records showed more than 400 children in one township had lost both parents to internment or prison, and children were assessed for 'centralised care'. School rules imposed points-based punishments on pupils and teachers for speaking anything other than Chinese. Zenz found evidence that children of detainees were being channelled into the boarding system in large numbers. The New York Times reported in December 2019 that about 497,000 pupils were enrolled in such schools. A Xinjiang propaganda official denied that the state was caring for large numbers of parentless children. No sexual-abuse finding is recorded here; this is a child-removal record.

cases.title: Myanmar → China — Kachin women and girls sold as 'brides' (HRW 2019)
cases.who: Traffickers including relatives and acquaintances; buying families in China
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's 112-page report of 21 March 2019 documented women and girls from Kachin and northern Shan States, many displaced by conflict, sold for US$3,000–13,000 to Chinese families, locked up and raped so they would become pregnant. patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 2025: law: Greece restores citizenship for about 4,000 Greek-born adoptees sent abroad 1950–1975 (2 May)
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption moved from one sending country to the next as each was exposed. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad from 1953 to 2008; its Truth and Reconciliation Commission found in 2025 that the state was responsible for human rights violations in those adoptions. Romania (1990s), Guatemala (until 2007–08), Cambodia and Vietnam, Nepal, Ethiopia (banned 2018) and others followed, each closed after inquiries found children bought, stolen or registered as orphans. Receiving countries then began to look at themselves: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after the Joustra committee, and China ended it in 2024. The map colors each sending country by whether it was later closed or suspended and draws 59 documented flows.

patterns.pattern: Governments that took children
patterns.role_note: Greece — about 4,000 children adopted abroad 1950–1975; 2025 citizenship law.
patterns.pattern_summary: Some of the largest removals of children were carried out by states, as policy. Argentina's junta took about 500 babies from detained mothers in 1976–83 (a 2012 court found a "systematic plan"; 140 grandchildren had been identified by July 2025). Under Franco, children were taken from Republican and later unmarried mothers. Canada, Australia and the United States removed Indigenous children into residential schools and non-Indigenous families; Denmark sent Greenlandic children to Danish families in 1951; France moved children from Réunion to rural France. Since 2022 Russia has deported Ukrainian children; the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in March 2023 for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova over it.

cases.title: Greece — about 4,000 children adopted abroad 1950–1975; 2025 citizenship law
cases.who: Greek state institutions and foundling homes; AHEPA and other US agencies and proxy-adoption intermediaries
cases.what: Between 1950 and 1975 as many as 4,000 Greek-born children, many called 'orphans' after the civil war or born 'illegitimate', were adopted in the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden through hastily conducted procedures. A law published on 2 May 2025 recognised their adopted status, restored a path to Greek citizenship and eased access to records. The Greek state promised an investigation in the late 1950s that has not been carried out.
cases.cover_up: The adoptions were covered by confidentiality and secrecy; many adoptees lacked papers proving their origins.

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Lechaina Children's Care Centre, Greece — caged beds and sedation
cases.who: State Children Care Center of Lechaina (children with disabilities)
cases.what: In March 2011 the Greek Ombudsman's Office published a report on the state care centre at Lechaina finding too few doctors and nurses, systematic sedation, residents tied to their beds and the use of wooden cage beds because of staff shortages; most children received no education. In 2012 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child expressed deep concern about the centre. A BBC report in 2014 found conditions had barely improved. This is a record of institutional abuse and neglect; no sexual-abuse finding was located.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Guatemala — notary-run adoption trade to the US (1996–2007)
cases.who: Private notaries (notarios), baby brokers, foster homes, officials
cases.what: After the civil war ended in 1996, adoptions abroad rose each year, run almost entirely (about 98%) by private notaries who handled both sides without court review and charged $35,000 or more per child; 97% of children went to the US. CICIG's 2010 report studied 153 cases and found 78% violated the new law in some way. Guatemala passed a Hague-compliant law on 11 December 2007 and stopped new adoptions to the US from 1 January 2008; the US State Department announced on 9 January 2008 it would not allow new adoptions until procedures were compliant.

cases.title: Guatemala — Casa Quivira raid: 46 children possibly stolen for adoption
cases.who: Casa Quivira private adoption home (run by a US citizen and his Guatemalan wife); two lawyers
cases.what: On 11 August 2007 Guatemalan police found 46 children aged a few days to three years at the Casa Quivira adoption home in Antigua after neighbours reported foreigners collecting children daily. Two lawyers who allegedly processed the adoptions were arrested. Attorney General Mario Gordillo said most of the children lacked proper documents and his office was investigating whether they had been stolen or obtained from mothers under coercion.

cases.title: Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción — abuse, trafficking alerts and fire killing 41 girls
cases.who: State-run children's home under the Secretariat of Social Welfare (SBS); National Civil Police
cases.what: About 700 children lived at the state home, built for a maximum of 500; most had committed no crime. Months before the fire prosecutors had recommended closing it over abuse allegations, and girls had protested overcrowding and alleged sexual abuse by staff. After an escape on 7 March 2017, police returned a group of girls and locked them in a room; on 8 March one girl set a mattress alight, killing 41 girls and injuring 15. The social welfare secretary, his deputy and the home's director were sacked and later charged. On 12 Aug 2025 a judge convicted six former officials of offences from manslaughter to abuse of authority, with sentences of 6 to 25 years; former secretary Carlos Rodas received 25 years and a police officer who held the key 13 years. The judge said the fire was the culmination of reported abuses not acted on, and ordered an investigation of former President Jimmy Morales.
cases.cover_up: Officials ignored repeated complaints: in November 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman asked the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights for precautionary measures citing mistreatment and a trafficking network recruiting children from the home. On the day of the fire police guarding the locked room did not let the girls out.
